title: Read a .gitignore file
prompt:
A `.gitignore` file lists patterns for files Git should ignore, and Git skips blank lines and lines that start with `#` [py-149]. Build a small Python model of that, using our own simplified matching rules.

`read_patterns(text)` turns the file's text into a list of patterns. `is_ignored(name, patterns)` says whether a file name matches one. The example file is `gitignore_example.txt` (a plain text copy with an ordinary file name).

When it works, `python3 ignore.py` prints the three patterns and then which of four shop files would be ignored.
expected_output:
['.venv', 'scratch.txt', '*.bak']
tracker.py False
.venv True
prices.bak True
scratch.txt True
hints: In `read_patterns`, walk through `text.split("\n")` one line at a time and keep only the lines you want in a new list.
Skip a line when it is empty or when `line.startswith("#")` is true [py-160]. Use `continue` to move on to the next line.
In `is_ignored`, loop over the patterns. Return `True` when `name == pattern`, or when the pattern starts with `"*"` and `name.endswith(pattern[1:])`. After the loop, return `False`.
explain_after:
The rule about blank lines and `#` comes from the Pro Git book [py-149]. The star rule is our own simplification for this exercise.

The `.venv` line matters for your showcase project. A virtual environment is created on top of a base Python [py-112], so you can build a fresh one on any machine. Its folder does not need a place in the logbook.
